statement: A bag holds 7 red, 5 blue and 2 green marbles. Without looking, Leo takes marbles out one at a time. What is the smallest number of marbles he must take to be sure of having at least one marble of each colour?

choices.misconception: I thought 3 marbles are enough because there are 3 colours, but all 3 could be red.
I used one more than the number of colours, which is how many you need to be sure of two marbles of the same colour, not one of each.
I only imagined taking all 7 reds first, and forgot that the next marble could be blue rather than green.
I found the unluckiest case, all 7 red and all 5 blue marbles, but forgot that he needs one more marble to get a green one.

hints: Imagine Leo is as unlucky as possible.
Find the largest number of marbles he could take and still be missing a colour. To be sure, he needs one more than that.
The unluckiest start is all of the two biggest colours: 7 red and 5 blue marbles, and still no green.

solutions.reliable: In the unluckiest case Leo first takes all 7 red and all 5 blue marbles: 12 marbles and no green. The next marble must be green, so 13 marbles are enough. Fewer are not: with 12 marbles he might still have no green. Any 13 marbles must contain every colour, because leaving out one colour leaves at most 7 + 5 = 12 marbles. The transferable idea: to guarantee something, build the unluckiest case that avoids it, then add one.

whyOnTest: Guarantee questions test worst-case thinking: find the unluckiest run that avoids the goal, then add one.
